## Intended scope

Public policy is often analyzed with tools built for aggregates — averages, totals, regression coefficients — that can obscure how outcomes actually propagate through networks of institutions, organizations, and people. This essay will outline:

- Where network structure (rather than aggregate statistics) plausibly matters for how public programs succeed or fail.
- A short, non-technical introduction to a few core network concepts (e.g., centrality, connectivity, community structure) aimed at a public-policy audience.
- Concrete, publicly documentable examples of network-analytic thinking applied to administrative or institutional networks.
- Open questions connecting this to the [current research questions](../../research.qmd#current-research-questions) on this site.
